claim_verdicts.evidence: "A *thread* is the basic unit to which an operating system allocates processor time. ... Multiple threads can run in the context of a process." and "By default, a .NET program is started with a single thread, often called the *primary* thread. However, it can create additional threads to execute code in parallel or concurrently with the primary thread." Both halves of the claim (at least one thread, can ask for more) are stated.

"All threads of a process share its virtual address space. A thread can execute any part of the program code, including parts currently being executed by another thread." A shared address space includes the heap the lesson names, and nothing is copied between threads.

API page, defaultMoniker net-10.0, Run(Action): "Queues the specified work to run on the thread pool and returns a Task object that represents that work." Pool side: "The ThreadPool class provides your application with a pool of worker threads that are managed by the system". Execution settles the "calling thread carries on" half: in 9 runs the caller reached the await and both queued loops ran, losing 44349-99969 increments.
claim_verdicts.source: learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.task.run (view=net-10.0), Overloads table; refs/dotnet-docs/docs/standard/threading/the-managed-thread-pool.md line 15; examples/don-hang (9 executed runs)

claim_verdicts.evidence: CS1686 guidance: "The compiler moves captured variables to a heap-allocated closure object, making their address unstable." Capture, not copy. The .NET 10 nuance does not apply here: "Objects 'escape' when assigned to non-local variables or passed to functions not inlined by the JIT. If an object can't escape, it can be allocated on the stack." The two closures are passed to Task.Run, so they escape and stay on the heap; execution confirms one shared counter (totals below 200000).
claim_verdicts.source: refs/dotnet-docs/docs/csharp/language-reference/compiler-messages/lambda-expression-errors.md line 171; docs/core/whats-new/dotnet-10/runtime.md line 204; examples/don-hang (9 executed runs)

claim_verdicts.evidence: "A simple example of a race condition is incrementing a field. ... This operation requires loading the value from objCt into a register, incrementing the value, and storing it in objCt." "a thread that has loaded and incremented the value might be preempted by another thread which performs all three steps; when the first thread resumes execution and stores its value, it overwrites objCt without taking into account the fact that the value has changed in the interim."

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- threads-vs-async` nine times on SDK 10.0.300. Counters: 148572, 113428, 100031, 153132, 155651, 106078, 118259, 151618, 141380 — all below 200000, no two equal. The upper bound follows from the documented mechanism: every write stores a value that was read plus one, so an increment can be lost but never invented.

WhenAll half is documented: "The Task.WhenAll method asynchronously waits for multiple Task or Task<TResult> objects to finish." The "as any await does" universal is contradicted on the await page: "When the await operator is applied to the operand that represents an already completed operation, it returns the result of the operation immediately without suspension of the enclosing method." Two 100000-iteration loops can finish before this line is reached, in which case no thread is handed back there.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: await Task.WhenAll(first, second) continues only once both supplied tasks have completed; unless they are already finished when the await is reached, it hands the thread back until then.

claim_verdicts.evidence: "An await expression in an async method doesn't block the current thread while the awaited task is running. Instead, the expression signs up the rest of the method as a continuation and returns control to the caller of the async method." That is the claim's two halves: the thread is not held for the wait, and the remainder is recorded as a continuation. Note the docs say control returns to the caller — not that the thread returns to a pool; see the section 3 issue.

Word for word: "The async and await keywords don't cause extra threads to be created. Async methods don't require multithreading because an async method doesn't run on its own thread. ... You can use Task.Run to move CPU-bound work to a background thread" — which is exactly the exception the claim names for the two Task.Run calls in the sample.

"The Task.Delay method produces a Task object that finishes after the specified time." "finishes after" supports the hedge "about". Non-blocking half: "An await expression in an async method doesn't block the current thread while the awaited task is running." Nine runs completed the pause and printed the line after it.

"Console apps don't install a SynchronizationContext, which means await continuations run on the thread pool." "In a console app, SynchronizationContext.Current returns null. When a method yields at an await, the continuation runs on whatever thread pool thread is available." Execution agrees: all nine runs printed "start, on thread 2" and then thread 4 or 6.
Property page, defaultMoniker net-10.0: "Gets a unique identifier for the current managed thread." Property Value: "A unique identifier for this managed thread." The claim is that sentence.

claim_verdicts.evidence: "the thread doesn't block while the eggs or hash browns are cooking, but the code also doesn't start other tasks until the current work completes. You still put the bread in the toaster and stare at the toaster until the bread pops up" — awaits written in turn happen in turn, so their durations add; starting the tasks before awaiting them is presented as the separate technique that overlaps them.

The mechanism is documented: "If any process is blocked in a synchronous application, all are blocked. Your application stops responding, and you might conclude that it failed when instead it's just waiting." The frequency word "often" is not: grepped refs/dotnet-docs for any ranking or share of causes of unresponsive UIs — nothing. Kind is opinion and the sentence carries its condition (programs with a screen), so no issue is raised.

Execution settles the overlap: nine runs lost 44349-99969 increments, which is only possible if the two loops ran at the same time on a machine running them simultaneously. Docs give the mechanism and the reason for "usually": "The ThreadPool class provides your application with a pool of worker threads that are managed by the system"; "If all thread pool threads are busy, additional work items are queued until threads to execute them become available."

"When you write server programs, you don't want to block threads that might be serving other requests. Using synchronous code when asynchronous alternatives exist hurts your ability to scale out less expensively. You pay for blocked threads." With the pool side: "the thread pool limits the number of threads that can be active in the process simultaneously. If all thread pool threads are busy, additional work items are queued until threads to execute them become available." The claim carries the condition those quotes describe.

"If your code implements I/O-bound scenarios to support network data requests, database access, or file system read/writes, asynchronous programming is the best approach" — the lesson's three examples are exactly that category, set against CPU-bound work; and "Should the code wait for a result or action, such as data from a database? — I/O-bound: Use the async modifier and await expression without the Task.Run method." Nothing is computed while such a wait is in flight, which is the sense the claim uses.

First half exact: "You can use the await operator only in a method, lambda expression, or anonymous method that is modified by the async keyword." Second half too strong: the async page lists Task, Task<TResult>, void and "Any type that has an accessible GetAwaiter method", and only advises "Use Task if the method returns no meaningful value when it completes." A value-less async method may be async void, whose caller "can't await it" — the case the claim's last clause denies.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A method must carry the async modifier for await to appear in its body; an async method that produces no value normally returns a Task standing for the work in flight, which its caller can await (async void exists for event handlers and cannot be awaited).

issues.text: Unlisted claim: the Core concepts entry says await hands the thread back "to the pool it came from". The thread that reaches the sample's first await did not come from a pool: a probe run of the same shape of code on SDK 10.0.300 printed "start id=2 pool=False" then "mid id=6 pool=True", so the entry thread reports IsThreadPoolThread false. The docs put it differently: await "signs up the rest of the method as a continuation and returns control to the caller of the async method" — no pool. Also false for a UI thread. No ledger claim covers it.
issues.fix: Drop the unconditional pool: "**async/await** — a way of writing a wait so the thread running the method is handed back — to the pool, if it came from one — while nothing is happening, and the rest of the method continues once the answer arrives." Add it to the ledger as a behavior claim sourced to task-asynchronous-programming-model.md line 122.

issues.text: "the method continues on whatever thread is free" is stated without condition. It holds because this is a console program: "Console apps don't install a SynchronizationContext, which means await continuations run on the thread pool", whereas "UI frameworks like Windows Forms, WPF, and .NET MAUI install a SynchronizationContext on their UI thread. When you await a task in those environments, the continuation automatically posts back to the UI thread." The lesson invokes programs with a screen one section later. Claim 11 carries the console condition; the body does not.
issues.fix: Condition the sentence on this program: "When the wait ends, the method continues on whatever thread is free — in a program like this one, with no screen — which is why the last line can print a different number."
issues.quote: When the wait ends, the method continues on whatever thread is free, which is why the last line can print a different number.
